intro.title: Counts and percentages
intro.bodyMarkdown:
This quest is about **summarising**: turning a table of rows into a few numbers that tell its story. The first question is usually "how many of each?", and for a column of categories, `table()` answers it.

```
orders <- data.frame(
  order = 101:110,
  day = c("Mon", "Mon", "Tue", "Tue", "Tue", "Wed", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Fri"),
  drink = c("latte", "tea", "mocha", "latte", "latte", "tea", "chai", "latte", "mocha", "tea"),
  size = c("M", "S", "L", "M", "S", "M", "L", "L", "M", "S"),
  price = c(3.4, 2.5, 4.2, 3.4, 2.9, 2.5, 3.8, 3.9, 4.2, 2.2)
)
```

```
table(orders$drink)
table(orders$size)
```

Counts are hard to compare between groups of different sizes, so we often report **percentages** instead. `prop.table()` turns counts into shares that add up to 1; multiply by 100 and round:

```
round(prop.table(table(orders$drink)) * 100)
```

Rounded percentages don't always add up to exactly 100. That's normal; say so in a report, or show one decimal place instead.

For a TRUE/FALSE question about each row, the share is simply the `mean()`: `mean(orders$price > 3)` is the share of orders over 3, because TRUE counts as 1. Multiply by 100 for a percentage.

Use a factor with ordered levels when the order matters, such as sizes S, M, L: `table(factor(orders$size, levels = c("S", "M", "L")))`.

intro.title: Centre: mean and median
intro.bodyMarkdown:
A "typical" value for a column of numbers is called its **centre**. The two you will use most are the mean and the median. This stage uses a bakery's delivery times:

```
deliveries <- data.frame(
  rider = c("Sam", "Ola", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Kit", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit"),
  area = c("north", "south", "north", "north", "south", "south", "north", "south", "south", "north", "north", "south"),
  minutes = c(24, 31, 19, 27, 35, 29, 22, 74, 33, 21, 26, 38)
)
```

The **mean** adds everything up and divides by the count. The **median** is the middle value when they are sorted. Here the mean is about 31.6 minutes but the median is 28: one delivery took 74 minutes (a flat tyre), and that single value pulls the mean up.

```
mean(deliveries$minutes)      # 31.58
median(deliveries$minutes)    # 28
```

Which to report? When values are fairly even, the mean and median are close and the mean is fine. When a few values are extreme, as with delivery times, incomes or house prices, the median describes the typical case better. Reporting both is often the most honest.

A **trimmed mean** is a middle way: `mean(x, trim = 0.1)` drops the lowest and highest 10% of values before averaging.

And always remember `na.rm = TRUE` when a column has gaps, or the answer is `NA`.

intro.title: Spread: sd, IQR and quantile
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Two bakeries can both average 30 minutes per delivery, one always 28 to 32, the other anywhere from 10 to 60. The centre is the same, the **spread** very different. These measure spread:

| Function | Gives |
| --- | --- |
| `range(x)` | the smallest and largest value |
| `sd(x)` | the standard deviation: roughly, how far values typically are from the mean |
| `var(x)` | the variance, `sd(x)` squared |
| `quantile(x, 0.9)` | the value 90% of the data is below |
| `IQR(x)` | the interquartile range: the spread of the middle half |

```
deliveries <- data.frame(
  rider = c("Sam", "Ola", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Kit", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit"),
  area = c("north", "south", "north", "north", "south", "south", "north", "south", "south", "north", "north", "south"),
  minutes = c(24, 31, 19, 27, 35, 29, 22, 74, 33, 21, 26, 38)
)
```

```
range(deliveries$minutes)                  # 19 74
round(sd(deliveries$minutes), 1)          # 14.6
quantile(deliveries$minutes)               # 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%
IQR(deliveries$minutes)                    # 10
```

`quantile()` without a second argument gives the **quartiles**: the values a quarter, half and three quarters of the way through the sorted data. The 50% quartile is the median. The IQR is the 75% quartile minus the 25% one, so it covers the middle half of the data.

Like the median, the IQR isn't pulled about by one extreme value, while the standard deviation is. Here the 74-minute delivery makes the sd 14.6, though the middle half of deliveries are within 10 minutes of each other.

Quantiles answer practical questions: "90% of deliveries arrive within how many minutes?" is `quantile(minutes, 0.9)`. All of these take `na.rm = TRUE`.

intro.title: Group summaries with tapply()
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Most real questions compare groups: which compost grows taller seedlings? Which rider is fastest? You could filter each group and summarise it, one at a time. `tapply()` does them all at once.

This stage uses a seedling trial: twelve trays, three kinds of compost, and each seedling's height after three weeks.

```
seedlings <- data.frame(
  tray = 1:12,
  compost = c("peat", "peat", "peat", "peat", "leaf", "leaf", "leaf", "leaf", "home", "home", "home", "home"),
  height_cm = c(8.2, 7.5, 9.1, 8.0, 10.4, 11.2, 9.8, 10.9, 7.1, 12.8, 6.9, 7.6),
  leaves = c(6, 5, 7, 6, 8, 9, 7, 8, 5, 9, 4, 5)
)
```

`tapply(values, groups, function)` splits the values by group and applies the function to each part:

```
tapply(seedlings$height_cm, seedlings$compost, mean)
#  home  leaf  peat
# 8.600 10.575 8.200
```

The result is a named vector, one value per group, in alphabetical order (or factor-level order). Everything you know about named vectors works on it: `round()`, `sort()`, `which.max()`, picking by name.

Any summary function works: `median`, `max`, `sd`, `length` (to count), `sum`. Extra arguments go at the end: `tapply(x, g, mean, na.rm = TRUE)`.

Look at the home compost: its mean is 8.6 but its median is only 7.35, because one tray grew to 12.8 cm. Comparing groups by their median as well as their mean helps you spot that.

intro.title: Summary tables with aggregate()
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`tapply()` gives a named vector. When you want the summary as a **data frame**, ready to sort, merge or print as a table, use `aggregate()`. It is written with a **formula**: what to summarise, a tilde `~`, and what to group by.

```
deliveries <- data.frame(
  rider = c("Sam", "Ola", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Kit", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit"),
  area = c("north", "south", "north", "north", "south", "south", "north", "south", "south", "north", "north", "south"),
  minutes = c(24, 31, 19, 27, 35, 29, 22, 74, 33, 21, 26, 38)
)
```

```
aggregate(minutes ~ rider, data = deliveries, FUN = mean)
```

Read `minutes ~ rider` as "minutes by rider". The result has one row per rider and two columns, `rider` and `minutes`.

Group by two columns with `+`, and get one row for every combination that appears: `aggregate(minutes ~ rider + area, data = deliveries, FUN = mean)` gives each rider's mean in each area.

Because the result is a data frame, you can sort it like any other: `res[order(res$minutes), ]`. Give the summary column a clearer name with `names(res)[2] <- "avg_minutes"`.

Formulas with `~` appear all over R's statistics, including the regression models in the last quest, so it is worth getting used to reading them.

intro.title: Two-way tables
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Give `table()` two columns and it counts every **combination**: a two-way table, also called a cross-tab. Rows are the values of the first column, columns the values of the second.

```
deliveries <- data.frame(
  rider = c("Sam", "Ola", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Kit", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit"),
  area = c("north", "south", "north", "north", "south", "south", "north", "south", "south", "north", "north", "south"),
  minutes = c(24, 31, 19, 27, 35, 29, 22, 74, 33, 21, 26, 38)
)
```

```
tab <- table(deliveries$rider, deliveries$area)
tab
```

Each cell is a count: Sam made 3 deliveries in the north and 1 in the south. Pick a cell with `tab["Sam", "north"]`, a row with `tab["Sam", ]`.

`addmargins(tab)` adds row and column totals, labelled `Sum`. For percentages, `prop.table()` needs to know what to divide by. `margin = 1` divides each **row** by its row total ("of Sam's deliveries, how many were north?"); `margin = 2` divides each **column** by its column total ("of the north deliveries, how many were Sam's?"):

```
round(prop.table(tab, margin = 1) * 100)   # each row adds up to 100
```

Two-way tables are the basis of the chi-squared test in the Statistics quest, which asks whether two categories are related.

intro.title: Spotting outliers
intro.bodyMarkdown:
An **outlier** is a value far from the rest. It may be a mistake (a typo, a sensor fault) or something real and interesting (the flat tyre). Either way, you want to find it before it quietly skews your averages.

A common rule, used by box plots, is based on the IQR. A value is an outlier if it is more than **1.5 × IQR** below the first quartile or above the third:

```
deliveries <- data.frame(
  rider = c("Sam", "Ola", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Kit", "Ola", "Kit", "Sam", "Ola", "Kit"),
  area = c("north", "south", "north", "north", "south", "south", "north", "south", "south", "north", "north", "south"),
  minutes = c(24, 31, 19, 27, 35, 29, 22, 74, 33, 21, 26, 38)
)
```

```
m <- deliveries$minutes
q1 <- quantile(m, 0.25)       # 23.5
q3 <- quantile(m, 0.75)       # 33.5
upper <- q3 + 1.5 * IQR(m)    # 48.5
lower <- q1 - 1.5 * IQR(m)    # 8.5
m[m > upper | m < lower]      # 74
```

R can do the whole calculation for you: `boxplot.stats(m)$out` gives the values the rule flags.

Another way is the **z-score**: how many standard deviations a value is from the mean, `(m - mean(m)) / sd(m)`. Values beyond about 2 or 3 are unusual. But an outlier also pushes up the sd it is measured against, so the IQR rule is often the better first check.

Finding an outlier is the start, not the end. Look at the whole row (`deliveries[m > upper, ]`), find out what happened, and then decide: fix it, leave it out with a note, or keep it and report the median.

intro.title: A summary report
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The point of a summary is to tell someone something. A few well-formatted lines often say more than a printed table. This stage puts the quest together into short reports, using a class's test results:

```
class_results <- data.frame(
  student = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cy", "Dee", "Eli", "Fay", "Gus", "Hal", "Ivy", "Jo", "Kai", "Lea"),
  group = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"),
  test1 = c(72, 65, 88, 54, 91, 47, 76, 69, 83, 58, 64, 95),
  test2 = c(78, 70, 85, 61, 94, NA, 80, 66, 88, 62, 71, 97)
)
```

Three tools do most of the formatting. `round()` keeps numbers readable. `sprintf()` gives exact control: `sprintf("%.1f", x)` always shows one decimal, and `sprintf("%5.1f", x)` lines numbers up in a column 5 wide. `cat()` puts it on the screen, and `sep = ""` stops it adding spaces.

```
m <- mean(class_results$test1)
cat(sprintf("Test 1: mean %.1f, median %.1f\n", m, median(class_results$test1)))
```

For a line per group, compute the summaries first (with `tapply()` or `aggregate()`), then give the whole vectors to `sprintf()`: it makes one line per value. `cat(…, sep = "")` then prints them one under another.

```
avg <- tapply(class_results$test1, class_results$group, mean)
cat(sprintf("Group %s: %.1f\n", names(avg), avg), sep = "")
```

A good report says what was measured, how many values it is based on, and anything surprising, such as missing values or an outlier.
